Where is Bella Vista and what is the town like?

Bella Vista is a city in the far northern part of Benton County, Arkansas, with its northern border on the Missouri state line. Wikipedia places it on the Springfield Plateau of the Ozarks, at an elevation of 1,204 feet.

The city covers 46.874 square miles, and 1.570 of them are water, mostly lakes. The 2020 census counted 30,104 residents with a median age of 51.0, and 31.3 percent of residents were 65 or older. Roughly 17.7 percent were under 18.

The city is largely residential and works as a bedroom community for Bentonville and Rogers. The page lists a median household income of $85,932 in the 2023 American Community Survey and a sales tax rate of 9.5 percent.

How did Bella Vista begin as a resort and retirement town?

Bella Vista started as a small summer resort in the early 20th century and became a retirement community in 1965. Lake Bella Vista was created in 1915 by damming Little Sugar Creek, and in 1916 the Linebarger Brothers Realty Company bought the resort and added the Sunset Hotel and the Wonderland Cave nightclub.

Cooper Communities developed the 1965 retirement community, and a property owners' association provided services and amenities. Residents voted on November 7, 2006 to incorporate, and the city took effect January 1, 2007, taking over police, fire, streets and trash removal.

That history explains something every seller here deals with: two layers of rules. One is city government. The other is the private property owners' association.

What is the difference between the city and the Bella Vista POA?

The city is a public government, and the Property Owners Association is a private nonprofit corporation. The city's legal FAQ says none of your POA dues go to the city, which is paid for by sales tax, property tax, state and county turnback funds, and city permit and license fees.

The two rule sets can conflict. Something a city ordinance allows may still break the covenants, and the POA can respond with lawsuits or sanctions. The reverse also happens, and then the city can cite you into court. The city does not interpret private covenants and suggests a private attorney for questions.

Dues are part of the sale. The city's residential building FAQ listed annual fees as of 2023 at $16 per month for unimproved lots and $40 per month for improved lots, and it tells sellers to verify unpaid dues with the POA at 479-855-8000.

Ask the POA for a statement of what you owe before you set a closing date.

  • Septic: request percolation test records from the Benton County Health Department at 479-986-1300 to see whether the lot passed.
  • Sewer: connection is required by city ordinance where sewer is available.
  • Water: connection to the POA is required within POA boundaries.

The same page says RVs are not allowed in residential areas unless fully screened from public view, and that fences may be up to 8 feet tall. The Architectural Control Committee enforces POA covenants, which typically address appearance.

Do you need a permit to repair a house in Bella Vista?

Residential building permits come from the city's Community Development office, reachable at 479-268-4980. Permits are valid for 180 days, and each scheduled inspection extends the permit another 180 days.

The Building Official can issue a stop work order to bring a project into line with codes. Septic permits come from the Benton County Health Department, and a pool needs a permit checklist plus an electrician's permit if electrical work is involved.

Code enforcement lists building without a permit among the common violations, along with overnight parking in yards or on streets, unsightly conditions, sign problems, trash service violations and illegal dumping. Reports go to 479-855-3771. The division does not handle disputes between neighbors.

If you have done work without a permit, find out where that stands with Community Development before you sell, and tell any buyer about it.

Bella Vista taxes are assessed by Benton County, whose assessor is Roderick Grieve at 2109 W. Walnut St. in Rogers, phone 479-271-1033. The state's 2025 report shows Benton's reappraisal cycle ending in 2028, done in house across 166,662 parcels.

Benton County was created September 30, 1836 as Arkansas's 35th county. Its seat is Bentonville, and the economy is heavily influenced by Walmart, with J.B. Hunt headquartered in Lowell. The 2025 estimate for the county is 332,554 people.

For homesteads, Arkansas caps the yearly rise in taxable value at 5 percent and offers a credit of up to $500, rising to $600 for 2026 bills.

Interstate 49 was completed around Bella Vista in 2021, and the Bella Vista Bypass runs to the south and west, taking through traffic off U.S. 71. Highway 279 (Forest Hills Boulevard) and Highway 340 (Lancashire Boulevard) also serve the city.

Yes. The city incorporated on January 1, 2007 and is a public government, while the POA is a private nonprofit corporation that enforces its own covenants.

Where is Benton, Arkansas, and what is the city like?

Benton is the county seat of Saline County and a suburb in the Little Rock-North Little Rock-Conway metro area. It sits at about 472 feet of elevation, and the Saline County Courthouse stands downtown.

The city's roots go back to the 1830s. It was named for Missouri senator Thomas Hart Benton, and early industry included a salt works that opened in 1827, kaolin pottery from about 1900, and logging and furniture making from the surrounding timber. Those older trades explain why parts of town have small mid-century frame houses next to newer subdivisions.

Growth has been steady for decades. The Census Bureau count for Benton went from 21,906 in 2000 to 30,681 in 2010 and 35,014 in 2020, with a July 2025 estimate of 38,898. In 2020 the city had 14,785 housing units, and 7.1 percent were vacant.

Benton has a humid subtropical climate, so the main wear on a house comes from heat, moisture and rain rather than snow. The July mean daily high is about 92.9 degrees Fahrenheit, and the record high is 112 degrees. January lows average near 30.6 degrees.

Confirm the district for a specific street before you advertise a house, since buyers with children usually ask. A house on a district boundary can pull different buyers than one a few blocks away.

Benton's Community Development office handles building permits and code enforcement from City Hall at 410 River Street. The office posts forms for residential remodels, accessory buildings, swimming pools, fences, retaining walls, grading, demolition and house moving, and it also lists floodplain forms.

Code enforcement covers overgrown lots, standing water, and abandoned or inoperable vehicles. The city says boats, trailers, farm implements and vehicles may not stay on public property more than seven consecutive days unless they are inside a building or tied to a licensed business, and it treats such violations as public nuisances. You can reach the office at 501-776-5938, and permit submissions go to permits@bentonar.gov. Hours are Monday to Friday, 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m.

How do property taxes work when you sell a house in Benton?

Saline County bills real estate tax one year behind, and the owner of record on the assessment date receives the bill. The county collector accepts payment from March 1 through October 15, and mailed payments must be postmarked by October 15. State law adds a 10 percent penalty to balances still unpaid after that date.

The collector's offices are in Benton and Bryant, open weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and the main number is 501-303-5620. State law also lets taxpayers pay in installments: one quarter by the third Monday in April, another quarter by the third Monday in July, and the final half by October 15.

A reappraisal is under way. Saline County says notices began arriving in July 2026 and go only to owners whose values rose. They are not tax bills, and the new values will not show up in this October's payment. Owners who disagree contact the assessor first, then the county equalization board.

At closing, the contract and the settlement statement decide how the year's bill is split between seller and buyer, so ask the title company to show the tax line. Getting around: where Benton sits for commuters and buyers

Saline County is crossed by Interstate 30 and its Business Loop, Interstate 530, U.S. Highways 65, 67, 70 and 167, and Arkansas Highways 5, 9 and 35. That road network is part of why the city works as a bedroom community for Little Rock workers.

Commute access shapes who buys. People who commute to Little Rock look at Benton because it is a county seat with its own downtown. If your house is close to an interchange or a main road, mention it plainly in any listing or cash-offer conversation.

What do sellers in Benton usually run into?

Sellers here tend to deal with the same few situations. A parent's house may have passed to several heirs. A rental may have tenants and deferred repairs. Some owners fall behind on a mortgage or tax bill, and others simply want to move without a round of showings.

The Arkansas homestead credit, available to owner-occupants, is worth knowing about if you are still living in the house. The Benton County assessor describes the statewide credit as up to $600 off the tax bill on a primary residence. Saline County's assessor can confirm how it applies to your house.

The deadline is October 15. The collector takes payments from March 1 through October 15, and a 10 percent penalty applies to unpaid balances after that date. Mailed payments need an October 15 postmark.

Do I need a permit or inspection to sell my Benton house?

A permit is not something this page can say is required for the sale itself, but any work done on the house should have been permitted. Benton's Community Development office issues permits for remodels, fences, pools and similar work. Ask them at 501-776-5938 if you are unsure about past work.

Can I sell a Benton house with code violations?

Yes. You can sell a house that has violations such as overgrown grass or stored vehicles, but open code issues can complicate a conventional sale. A cash buyer who buys as-is will usually take the house in its current condition. Contact Benton code enforcement to learn what is open on your address.

Where is Bentonville, Arkansas, and how did it grow?

The town was incorporated on April 3, 1873, and was first called Osage before it took the name of Missouri senator Thomas Hart Benton. The first railroad bypassed it and created Rogers instead, and in 1883 a local railroad company linked the two towns. In 1950 Sam Walton bought the Harrison Variety Store on the square, and Walton's 5 & 10 opened on March 18, 1951. That store led to Walmart.

It began in 1873 as a refueling stop on the Cairo and Fulton Railroad after the line bypassed nearby Austin, and it was incorporated on November 9, 1891.

Growth came in waves. The 1955 opening of Little Rock Air Force Base in Jacksonville brought families, and federal desegregation orders for the Little Rock School District in 1972 sent more to surrounding towns. Cabot's census population rose from 1,321 in 1960 to 8,319 in 1990, 15,261 in 2000, 23,776 in 2010 and 26,569 in 2020. The 2025 estimate is 27,711.

One event still shapes the downtown layout. A tornado struck Cabot on March 29, 1976, killing five people and destroying several buildings, and City Plaza was built on the rebuilt site. City Hall, the municipal courtroom and the police station now sit there.

The city also holds Cabotfest each October downtown and Strawberry Fest each spring, a nod to the strawberries once shipped from the area by rail. The city has 43 churches and two country clubs, Greystone on the north end and Rolling Hills in the southeast.

The city covers a little over 32 square miles, and its elevation is about 289 feet. U.S. 412 and U.S. 49 cross just west of downtown. Pine Bluff began as a river settlement after the flood of 1819 and was officially named by the county court on October 16, 1832. It was incorporated on January 8, 1839, and the first railroad arrived in December 1873.

Cotton and river trade made it the third-largest city in Arkansas by 1890. Jefferson County produced 55,120 bales of cotton in 1886, the most of any county in the state. Victorian-style houses were built west of Main Street as personal fortunes grew from the 1870s.

Pine Bluff's flat river-delta location means flood history is a fair question for any buyer. The Great Flood of 1927 flooded most of northern and southeastern Jefferson County and broke levees, and the 1933 Mississippi River flood displaced residents who relocated to Pine Bluff.

Where is Texarkana, Arkansas, and why is it a twin city?

Texarkana, Arkansas is the county seat of Miller County, in the southwest corner of the state, and it shares a state line with its twin city, Texarkana, Texas. It is 143 miles southwest of Little Rock, 72 miles north of Shreveport, Louisiana, and 180 miles northeast of Dallas.

The city covers about 42.2 square miles of flat Gulf Coastal Plain in the Piney Woods, an oak-hickory forest region. Together the two cities anchor a metro area of 147,174 residents as of 2021. The Federal Courthouse, which also houses the city's only post office, sits directly on the Arkansas-Texas line and is the only federal office building that straddles a state line.

For a seller the border has one plain consequence. A Texarkana mailing address does not tell you which state a parcel is in, and the state decides which tax, title and probate rules apply. This page covers the Arkansas side.

How did Texarkana, Arkansas, begin?

Town lots were sold at a railroad intersection on December 8, 1873, a date both cities generally recognize as their founding, and Texarkana, Texas was founded the next year. Miller County has an older and stranger history than the city. It was formed in 1820 in the Arkansas Territory, named for James Miller, the territory's first governor, and dissolved in 1838 with its land given to Lafayette County. The Arkansas legislature re-established it in 1874.

Arkansas incorporated the city in 1880, though the sources we read give two different dates in August and October. Population grew from 1,390 in 1880 to 29,919 in 2010 and slipped to 29,387 in 2020. The Census Bureau estimates 29,123 for July 1, 2025.

What do the Census figures show for Texarkana housing?

The median home value here is well under the figure for Sherwood or Springdale, and so is median household income. These are Census Bureau QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024.

Who are the major employers around Texarkana?

The largest single employer near Texarkana is the Red River Army Depot, which employs more than 3,500 people. The 2018 employer report lists these Texarkana-area employers:

  • Red River Army Depot, 4,135 workers
  • Christus St. Michael Health Care, 1,800
  • Cooper Tire and Rubber, 1,750
  • AECOM/URS, 1,300

The depot is about 18 miles west of the city in Bowie County, Texas. It was activated in 1941 as an ammunition storage site and now rebuilds Army vehicles and rocket systems on 15,375 acres. The Base Realignment and Closure Commission recommended closing it in 1995 and again in 2005, and it stayed open both times.

The city's economy began as a rail trading center and still rests on agriculture and trade. Miller County also has a strong industrial manufacturing base.

What roads and airport does Texarkana have?

Three interstates meet at Texarkana: I-30, I-49 and the future I-69. The average commute to work is 17.1 minutes.

Texarkana Regional Airport is three miles northeast of the city on 964 acres. It is a mixed-use field with mainly general aviation and limited commercial service. A new terminal opened on June 28, 2024, named for E-Z Mart founder Jim E. Yates. It has two asphalt runways, 6,601 and 5,200 feet.

What schools serve Texarkana, Arkansas?

The Texarkana Arkansas School District is the largest public district on the Arkansas side, and it feeds Arkansas High School. A very small part of the city lies in the Genoa Central School District. The University of Arkansas Hope-Texarkana opened as a branch campus in 2012, Texarkana College is on the Texas side, and Trinity Christian School is a private Baptist school for pre-K through grade 12.

If your house is near the city's edge, verify the school district on your parcel before you advertise it.

What weather and drainage issues affect Texarkana houses?

Texarkana has hot, humid summers, mild to cool winters, and about 48.9 inches of rain a year. Nix Creek is the main drainage, flowing into the Red River watershed. The land is flat, so a seller who knows where water collects on the lot can answer a buyer's inspector directly.

What is Miller County like beyond the city?

Miller County had 42,600 residents in the 2020 census, and Texarkana is its county seat. The county was recreated in December 1874 from part of Lafayette County. Its courthouse sits on land the railroad sold to the county for a nominal price on the condition that it be used for a courthouse.

The landscape is mostly forested rolling hills. The Red River forms the county's northern and western boundaries and is a popular fishing spot, and the 17,000-acre Sulphur River Wildlife Management Area is known for duck hunting. For a lot outside city limits, ask the county offices below which rules apply.

Common questions from sellers in this part of Arkansas include:

  • Whether the parcel is inside Texarkana city limits or in the county, which decides who issues permits.
  • Whether the house sits in the Texarkana Arkansas or Genoa Central school district.
  • Who holds title when a parent has died and no probate was opened.

Which city and county offices handle a Texarkana sale?

The city's Planning and Zoning Division sits within Public Works at 216 Walnut Street, and it reviews building permits, special use requests and zoning compliance. Call 870-779-4974 for Public Works or 870-779-4944 for the city planner. The Planning Commission, Historic District Commission and Board of Adjustment all meet under the city, and agendas are posted on the city's meeting portal. Texarkana uses a council-manager system.

The county offices are all at 400 Laurel Street, Texarkana, AR 71854:

  • Assessor, Suite 100, 870-774-1502
  • Collector, Suite 111, 870-774-1001
  • Treasurer, Suite 104, 870-774-0003
  • Circuit Clerk, Suite 109, 870-774-4501

Taxes in Arkansas are due October 15 each year. According to the Texarkana Gazette, real estate taxes that go unpaid can be certified to the Commissioner of State Lands, and the collector's office handles redemption questions at the number above. The Arkansas transfer tax on a deed is $3.30 per $1,000, so $330 on a $100,000 sale.

When does a cash sale make sense in Texarkana?

A cash sale suits owners who need a fixed closing date, who hold a house that would not pass a lender's appraisal, or who are settling an estate from out of town. A traditional listing may bring more on a well-kept house, so compare both. Cash Home Buyers buys houses as-is in Arkansas and writes an offer after learning the facts of the property.

More questions about Texarkana, AR

Is Texarkana, Arkansas the same as Texarkana, Texas?

No. They are twin cities on opposite sides of the state line, with separate city governments and different state laws. The Arkansas side is the county seat of Miller County.

How many people live in Texarkana, Arkansas?

The Census Bureau estimates 29,123 residents as of July 1, 2025. The 2020 census counted 29,387.

The Census Bureau reports $170,200 for owner-occupied homes from 2020 to 2024. It is a survey median, and a single house can sit well above or below it.

Where do I pay property tax in Miller County?

The Miller County Collector, Suite 111 at 400 Laurel Street, phone 870-774-1001. Arkansas real estate and personal property taxes are due October 15.

Which office handles building permits in Texarkana, Arkansas?

The city's Planning and Zoning Division within Public Works, at 216 Walnut Street. The Public Works number is 870-779-4974.

Yes. Cash buyers commonly purchase as-is, so you do not have to fix the roof, foundation or drainage before closing.
